results.content:
Title: Primary and Secondary Outcome Measures - PlanetMed
דף הבית » Blog » Primary and Secondary Outcome Measures. # Primary and Secondary Outcome Measures. Within this framework, primary and secondary outcome measures play a critical role, functioning as linchpins that connect the research question to reliable and interpretable results. ## **The Paramount Primary Outcome Measure**. The primary outcome measure represents the **pivotal** question a study seeks to answer. Here are key attributes of a robust primary outcome measure:. In a trial evaluating a novel pain medication, the primary outcome measure might be the mean decrease in pain score reported by participants. ## **The Supporting Ensemble: Secondary Outcome Measures**. While the primary outcome measure takes center stage, secondary outcome measures provide invaluable supplementary information. * **Long-Term Effects:** Secondary measures can track the intervention’s impact over a longer period, providing insights into its sustainability. * **Patient-Reported Outcomes (PROs):** These measures capture patients’ perspectives on their health and well-being. * **Exploratory Measures:** Secondary measures can also be used to investigate new hypotheses or gather data on less established outcomes. For instance, a study on a novel depression treatment might include a secondary measure to explore its potential effect on sleep quality. Selecting the most appropriate outcome measures demands thoughtful consideration. * **Study Objectives:** The measures must directly align with the research question. To ensure transparency and mitigate bias, it’s crucial to **pre-register** the primary and secondary outcome measures before initiating the study. While a single, robust primary outcome measure is ideal, sometimes using a **composite outcome** can be advantageous. For instance, a study on a weight-loss program might combine measures of weight change, body fat percentage, and waist circumference into a composite outcome. While outcome measures provide valuable quantitative data, it’s paramount to not lose sight of the human narrative behind the numbers. Integrating outcome measures with qualitative research methods, such as interviews or focus groups, can provide a more holistic understanding of the intervention’s effect on patients’ lives. Primary and secondary outcome measures serve as the foundation of well-designed medical research. By carefully selecting and defining these measures, researchers can navigate the intricacies of medical investigation and deliver clear, reliable evidence to guide clinical practice and ultimately improve patient care.

results.title: Preregistered - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics
results.content: Preregistration refers to the publicly available record of a researcher's (or research team's) questions, hypotheses, and method of investigation for a prospective study (Nosek et al., 2018). Preregistration is the process of registering a timestamped plan for a research project prior to collecting or observing the data (Tackett et al., 2019). The Open Science Framework (OSF) hosts preregistration templates for various research designs, including randomized controlled trials, secondary data analyses, qualitative research approaches, and quasi-experimental research studies (https://osf.io/prereg/). First, full preregistration encourages detailed attention to research study design prior to commencing data collection. Although SCD's data-analytic methods are less frequently concerned with NHST, some researchers have argued for the value of preregistration in a SCD context (e.g., Johnson & Cook, 2019), at least one research group has already begun publishing its study preregistrations for SCDs (i.e., Clanchy et al., 2019), and a registry for SCD preregistration is now available for general use (https://sreereg.icpsr.umich.edu).

results.title: Demystifying Primary Outcome Measures - CACHEducation
results.content: However, understanding primary outcome measures can be challenging for both patients and advocacy groups. In this article, we will be demystifying primary outcome measures and highlighting the significant role patient advocacy groups can play in informing them. Differences in perspectives between researchers, clinicians, regulators, and patients can make it quite difficult to reach a consensus on the most appropriate primary outcome measure in a clinical trial. #### How Patient Advocacy Groups Can Inform Primary Outcome Measures:. By actively engaging with researchers and clinical trial sponsors, patient advocacy groups can provide valuable insights into the lived experiences and priorities of patients. Patient advocacy groups can inform outcome measures in a number of ways:. * **By providing patient input.** Patient advocacy groups can facilitate patient engagement activities, such as focus groups, surveys, or interviews, to gather input on potential outcome measures. Patient advocacy groups can also advocate for the inclusion of patient-reported outcomes (PROs) as primary outcome measures, as they offer valuable insights into the subjective experiences and perceptions of patients. * **By participating in study designs.** Patient advocacy groups can actively participate in the design phase of clinical trials, including the selection of primary outcome measures. By actively engaging with researchers and clinical trial sponsors, patient advocacy groups can ensure that primary outcome measures are patient-centred, meaningful, and reflective of patients’ needs and preferences. Through collaborative efforts, researchers, clinicians, and patient advocacy groups can work together to improve the relevance and effectiveness of clinical research outcomes, ultimately benefiting patients and advancing medical knowledge and care. This course will educate students about the different entities in the Canadian health care system (Health Canada, CADTH, PMPRB, Provincial Ministries, pCPA, INESSS, etc) and how they interact with patient advocacy groups. #### Starting a Patient Advocacy Group. results.title: On the Importance of Subjective and Objective Measures - QS newcomers - Quantified Self Forum
results.content:
Title: On the Importance of Subjective and Objective Measures - QS newcomers - Quantified Self Forum
Subjective metrics (e.g. happiness) alone aren’t very consistent or reliable data points. Objective metrics (e.g. distance run) are great for statistical analysis but don’t yet exist for many of the things we care about. The latest version of my personal tracking framework has around 40 data points for both Subjective Productivity Rating (SPR) and for Deep Work hours. SPR is a measure of how productive my day was with reference to the things most important to my life and career, on an integer scale of 1–5. Deep Work hours are a related objective metric, simply measured by how many hours I logged in my retrospective calendar as being spent in a state of Deep Work. SPR is subject to bias, flawed perceptions and the inherent noisiness of quantifying a psychological experience, whilst Deep Work hours are only a reference point for how productive I was. If, as you point out, I am being *overly* pessimistic about the relevance of SPR as a metric, then I can always update my hypotheses to be more lenient. I should also point out that when cross-referencing the SPR data from previous datasets with my productivity score on RescueTime, there was also fairly low correlation. I’d love to know your thoughts on my choice of a 1-5 scale as opposed to 3-, 7-, or 10- point scales. The late Seth Roberts had a 100 point scale for sleep quality, which everybody gave him a hard time about. There were skeptical questions about it at nearly every talk, and while I learned a ton from Seth and respected his experience a lot, I myself was never convinced that he needed 100 points on that scale. I tend to care about extreme, easily noticed effects, so I use binary measures or three point scales most of the time. Around 80% of my actively tracked metrics are indeed binary. For SPR, SMR (subjective mood rating), general anxiety, and a few other metrics I use my 5-point scale. I can’t recall ever using 3-point metrics before. I’ve used a 3 pt scale for sleep quality, mood, and hunger.
